text_blocks.snippet: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is treated using a combination of lifestyle modifications and prescription medications, with a general blood pressure target of less than 130/80 mmHg.
Non-pharmacologic changes are the foundation of treatment and can help lower blood pressure or reduce the number of medications needed:

list.snippet: Dietary Changes: Follow the DASH (Diet Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet, which focuses on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy.
Sodium Reduction: Limit daily sodium intake to less than 1,500 mg per day.
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise (such as brisk walking) for at least 150 minutes per week.
Weight Management: Achieve and maintain a healthy weight.
Substance Limits: Limit alcohol consumption and quit smoking.
Sleep and Stress: Prioritize good sleep hygiene and manage stress.

text_blocks.snippet: When lifestyle changes are not enough—or immediately for Stage 2 hypertension (140/90 mmHg or higher) or high-risk patients—doctors prescribe one or more of these first-line drug classes:

list.snippet: Angiotensin-Receptor Blockers (ARBs): Relax blood vessels by blocking a hormone called angiotensin (e.g., losartan, valsartan); often favored if you have diabetes or kidney disease.
ACE Inhibitors: Prevent blood vessels from narrowing by stopping angiotensin production (e.g., lisinopril, enalapril).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells to let vessels relax (e.g., amlodipine, nifedipine).
Thiazide Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the body get rid of excess sodium and water (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone).

text_blocks.snippet: If blood pressure goals are not met with a single drug, providers often combine two or more medications at lower doses rather than raising to a high single dose. Other classes include:

list.snippet: Beta-Blockers: Slow the heart rate and reduce the force of pumping (e.g., metoprolol, carvedilol).
Mineralocorticoid/Aldosterone Antagonists: Used for resistant hypertension (e.g., spironolactone).
Alpha-Blockers and Vasodilators: Relax blood vessel walls when other options need supplementation.

text_blocks.snippet: You can read more detailed treatment guidelines through the Mayo Clinic High Blood Pressure Guide or review medication classes via the American Heart Association.
